categories.name: Fermented & Funky
categories.blurb: Time is the secret ingredient. Kimchi, doenjang, and the slow-built funk that starts it all.

categories.name: Charred & Smoky
categories.blurb: Fire meets flesh. Grilled, broiled, and blistered until the edges go black and sweet.

categories.name: Noodles & Broth
categories.blurb: Slurp-worthy strands and deep, layered bowls. Chewy, saucy, or swimming in broth.

categories.name: Rice & Bowls
categories.blurb: One bowl, everything in it. Crisp-bottomed rice built for mixing hard at the table.

categories.name: Small Plates & Banchan
categories.blurb: Snacks with swagger. Street food, banchan, and the plates you fight over.

categories.name: Braises & Stews
categories.blurb: Low and slow, bubbling and bold. The comfort corner, turned all the way up.

categories.name: Sweet Heat
categories.blurb: Sugar with a sting. Desserts and treats that finish on a slow ember.

dishes.name: Gochujang-Glazed Galbi Short Ribs
dishes.shortDesc: Fire-kissed short ribs lacquered in fermented chili and grated pear.
dishes.longDesc: Flanken-cut ribs bathe in gochujang, grated Korean pear, and toasted sesame until the sugars are ready to burn. A screaming-hot sear turns the marinade into glossy black lacquer with charred, caramel edges. Wrap each piece in lettuce and let the fermented heat do the talking.
method: Whisk gochujang, grated pear, garlic, soy, sesame oil, and honey into a loose glaze.
Coat the short ribs and marinate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
Heat a grill or cast-iron pan until it smokes.
Sear the ribs 2-3 minutes per side, basting with reserved glaze until lacquered and charred at the edges.
Rest 5 minutes, shower with scallions and toasted sesame, and serve with lettuce for wrapping.

dishes.name: Baechu Kimchi
dishes.shortDesc: The mother ferment—napa cabbage, gochugaru, and patient time.
dishes.longDesc: This is where Gochujang begins: napa cabbage salted, massaged with a scarlet paste of gochugaru, garlic, and fish sauce, then left to bubble. Over five days it turns sour, funky, and alive—the backbone of a dozen other dishes on this site. Make one batch and you'll never reach for the jarred stuff again.
method: Quarter the cabbage and salt between every leaf; rest 2 hours until pliable, then rinse and drain.
Cook rice flour with water into a loose porridge and cool—this feeds the ferment.
Blend gochugaru, garlic, ginger, fish sauce, and the porridge into a scarlet paste.
Fold in julienned radish and scallions, then massage the paste deep into every leaf (gloves on).
Pack tightly into a jar, press out the air, and leave at room temp 1-2 days until it bubbles.
Move to the fridge and let it deepen 3-5 days before the first sour, funky bite.

dishes.name: Rosé Tteokbokki
dishes.shortDesc: Chewy rice cakes in a blushing gochujang-cream sauce.
dishes.longDesc: Seoul's chewiest street snack, updated with a blush-pink sauce where gochujang meets cream and a whisper of bacon. The rice cakes turn pillowy and glossy—spicy but soothed, comfort with a low ember. It's the gateway drug of Korean food, and we're not sorry.
method: Soak the rice cakes in warm water 10 minutes so they turn pillowy.
Crisp the bacon, then bloom garlic, gochujang, and gochugaru in the rendered fat.
Pour in cream and milk and simmer into a blushing pink sauce.
Add the drained rice cakes and stir until glossy and coated, 5-6 minutes.
Finish with Parmesan and scallions and eat while molten.

dishes.name: Dolsot Bibimbap
dishes.shortDesc: Sizzling stone-bowl rice, seasoned vegetables, and a gochujang crown.
dishes.longDesc: Jeonju's signature bowl, built in a stone dish so hot the bottom layer of rice crackles into crisp nurungji. Each vegetable is seasoned on its own, then arranged in bright wedges around a molten egg and a bold spoon of gochujang. You mix it hard at the table—the ritual is half the pleasure.
method: Season each vegetable separately with sesame oil, salt, and garlic—this keeps the flavors distinct.
Rub a stone bowl with sesame oil and press in the warm rice.
Arrange the vegetables in bright wedges over the rice.
Heat the bowl until the bottom rice crackles into golden crust (nurungji).
Slide a fried egg on top, add a spoonful of gochujang, and mix hard at the table before every bite.

dishes.name: Doenjang Jjigae
dishes.shortDesc: Rustic fermented-soybean stew, deep, savory, endlessly comforting.
dishes.longDesc: The everyday Korean stew, anchored by doenjang—soybeans fermented into deep, savory funk. Tofu, zucchini, and potato simmer in anchovy-kelp stock until the whole pot tastes like home. Humble, fast, and quietly addictive.
method: Simmer anchovy-kelp stock and whisk in doenjang and a touch of gochujang until dissolved.
Add potato and cook until nearly tender.
Drop in zucchini, chili, and cubed tofu and simmer 8 minutes.
Scatter scallions and serve bubbling with a bowl of hot rice.

dishes.name: Yangnyeom Fried Chicken
dishes.shortDesc: Double-fried chicken shattering under a sticky gochujang glaze.
dishes.longDesc: Double-fried until the crust shatters like glass, then tossed in a sticky gochujang glaze that's equal parts sweet, tangy, and hot. This is the chicken that made Korean fried chicken a global obsession. Serve with cold beer and pickled radish; regret nothing.
method: Pat the wings bone-dry, toss with soy and a little starch, then dredge fully in potato starch.
Fry at 325°F until pale and cooked, about 8 minutes; rest, then fry again at 375°F until glass-crisp.
Simmer gochujang, ketchup, honey, garlic, and vinegar into a glossy glaze.
Toss the hot wings in glaze until every crag is lacquered.
Finish with toasted sesame and crushed peanuts; serve with pickled radish.

dishes.name: Buldak Fire Noodles
dishes.shortDesc: Chewy noodles in a searing gochujang-chili sauce. Bring water.
dishes.longDesc: The internet's favorite dare, made from scratch: thick noodles slicked in a gochujang-and-gochugaru lacquer stoked with cayenne. It's genuinely, gloriously punishing—a five-alarm rush chased with sweat and a grin. Melt mozzarella on top if you value your life.
method: Boil the noodles until just chewy and drain, saving a splash of the water.
Cook garlic in oil, then add gochujang, gochugaru, cayenne, soy, and honey into a fiery lacquer.
Toss the noodles in the sauce with a little pasta water until it clings.
Blanket with mozzarella if you need mercy, and finish with sesame and seaweed.

dishes.name: Gochujang Bolognese
dishes.shortDesc: Slow-braised ragù with a fermented-chili backbone over tagliatelle.
dishes.longDesc: Bologna's Sunday ragù with a Seoul accent: gochujang toasted into the soffritto for a fermented, umami-deep backbone. Two slow hours later the sauce is silky, meaty, and quietly complex, clinging to every ribbon of tagliatelle. Nobody will name the secret ingredient—they'll just ask for more.
method: Brown the meat hard in a heavy pot until deeply caramelized.
Add the soffritto—onion, carrot, garlic—and soften, then stir in gochujang to toast it.
Deglaze with red wine, add tomatoes and milk, and barely simmer 2 hours.
Cook the tagliatelle al dente and finish it in the ragù with a ladle of pasta water.
Shower with Parmesan; the ferment hums under the sweetness.

dishes.name: Kimchi Jjigae
dishes.shortDesc: Aged kimchi and pork belly simmered into sour, spicy comfort.
dishes.longDesc: When your kimchi turns too sour to eat straight, this is its second act: simmered with pork belly and tofu into a bubbling, brick-red stew. The funk mellows into something rich and deep, sharpened by gochujang and a hit of gochugaru. Serve it volcanic-hot with a bowl of white rice.
method: Sear the pork belly until the fat renders and crisps.
Add the kimchi and stir-fry until it darkens and smells deeply sour.
Stir in gochujang and gochugaru, then pour in stock and simmer 20 minutes.
Add sliced tofu and onion and cook until everything melds.
Scatter scallions and serve bubbling straight from the pot.

dishes.name: Gochujang Birria Tacos
dishes.shortDesc: Chili-braised beef tacos crisped in fat, dunked in gochujang consommé.
dishes.longDesc: A love letter between Jalisco and Seoul—beef chuck braised in guajillo adobo spiked with gochujang until it shreds at a glance. The tortillas get dipped in crimson fat, griddled crisp, and packed with molten cheese. Dunk each taco in the consommé and taste two chili traditions become one.
method: Toast the guajillos and blend with gochujang, garlic, onion, and cumin into a red adobo.
Coat the chuck and braise low with stock until fork-tender, about 3 hours.
Shred the beef and skim the crimson fat from the consommé.
Dip tortillas in the fat, fill with beef and cheese, and crisp on a hot griddle.
Serve golden and dripping with a bowl of consommé for dunking.

dishes.name: Gochujang-Miso Black Cod
dishes.shortDesc: Silky black cod glazed with gochujang and white miso, broiled to caramel.
dishes.longDesc: The Nobu trick, rerouted through a jar of gochujang: buttery black cod cured for two days in miso and fermented chili. Under the broiler the glaze blisters to bittersweet caramel while the flesh stays custard-soft. It looks like restraint and tastes like a secret.
method: Whisk miso, gochujang, mirin, sake, and sugar into a smooth cure.
Coat the fillets and rest, covered, 2 days in the fridge to firm and flavor the flesh.
Wipe off the excess and broil close to the flame until the glaze blisters and blackens at the edges.
Rest briefly; the flesh should flake in glossy, custardy petals.
Plate with a swipe of glaze and a few microgreens—restraint is the point.

dishes.name: Gochujang Shakshuka
dishes.shortDesc: Eggs poached in a smoky gochujang-tomato bath.
dishes.longDesc: Tel Aviv brunch meets Korean heat—eggs poached in a thick tomato bath deepened with smoky gochujang and cumin. The yolks stay jammy, the sauce clings to charred bread, and the fermented chili gives it a low, humming warmth. One pan, zero ceremony, total joy.
method: Soften the onion, pepper, and garlic, then toast the cumin and gochujang until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and simmer into a thick, brick-red sauce.
Make wells and crack in the eggs; cover and cook until the whites just set.
Crumble feta over the top and shower with cilantro.
Serve straight from the pan with charred bread for dragging.

dishes.name: Ssam with Ssamjang
dishes.shortDesc: Grilled pork wrapped in lettuce with a funky fermented dipping paste.
dishes.longDesc: The most communal way to eat in Korea: grilled pork belly, a lettuce leaf, a spoon of rice, and a dab of ssamjang—doenjang and gochujang blended into pungent, savory glue. You build each bite in your hand and eat it in one go. Loud, hands-on, and impossible to do politely.
method: Stir doenjang, gochujang, garlic, sesame oil, and honey into a thick ssamjang.
Grill the pork belly until the edges char and crisp.
Lay a leaf on your palm and add rice, a slice of pork, and a dab of ssamjang.
Top with raw garlic and chili, wrap into a bundle, and eat in one bold bite.

dishes.name: Gochujang Dark Chocolate Tart
dishes.shortDesc: Bittersweet ganache tart with a slow gochujang ember on the finish.
dishes.longDesc: A Parisian ganache tart with a Korean twist you feel before you can name it: gochujang steeped into the cream for a slow, smoldering finish. The chocolate is dark and bittersweet, the heat arrives a beat late, and flaky salt ties it together. Dessert for people who like a little danger.
method: Warm the cream with gochujang and honey until it just steams, then steep 5 minutes.
Pour the strained cream over chopped chocolate and let it melt, then whisk to a glossy ganache.
Whisk in the butter for shine and pour into the baked shell.
Chill until set, at least 3 hours.
Finish with flaky salt; the heat arrives a beat after the sweetness.

stories.title: The Slow Fire: Why Gochujang Takes a Year
stories.excerpt: Real gochujang isn't cooked—it's grown. We trace a single jar from steamed rice and chili powder through a full year of sun on a rooftop in Sunchang, and ask what patience actually tastes like.

stories.title: Seoul After Midnight: A Street-Food Crawl
stories.excerpt: From tteokbokki carts under neon to charcoal grills in a Gwangjang alley, we eat our way across the city between 11pm and dawn—and find the dishes worth flying for hiding in plastic-stool corners.

stories.title: The Case for Funk: Learning to Love Doenjang
stories.excerpt: It smells like a dare and tastes like the ocean floor in the best way. A field guide to fermented soybean paste—how it's made, why it reads as savory, and the three dishes that will convert you for good.
